analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $6.65 in two steps and extends it to the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a Senate vote: introduced with 37 cosponsors and placed on the Senate calendar, it sat there for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $5.15 to $5.90 an hour about two months after passage, then to $6.65 an hour a year later. It would also, for the first time, apply the federal minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, phasing the local wage up from $3.55 until it matches the federal rate. The bill was introduced by the Senate Democratic leader and placed on the Senate calendar, but it was never brought up for a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid the federal minimum wage of $5.15 an hour would see two raises, first to $5.90 and then to $6.65 [S2][S3]. Workers in the Northern Mariana Islands, where the federal minimum wage did not apply, would get a local minimum of $3.55 that rises every six months until it reaches the federal rate [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in two steps: to $5.90 an hour 60 days after enactment, and to $6.65 an hour 12 months after that [S2][S3].

For the first time applies the Fair Labor Standards Act minimum wage to the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, starting at $3.55 and rising 50 cents every six months until it matches the federal wage [S3].
The bill had broad support within its chamber: 37 senators signed on as cosponsors, 36 Democrats and one Independent, alongside the sponsor [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay minimum-wage workers — restaurants, retail stores, farms, and other low-wage businesses — would bear higher payroll costs, and some of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices. Employers in the Northern Mariana Islands, including its garment industry, would face a phased-in federal wage floor they had previously been exempt from [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: Employers of minimum-wage workers would face higher labor costs twice in about a year, which could lead to reduced hours, fewer entry-level jobs, or higher prices; this is the standard good-faith objection to a minimum wage increase.

The increases were not tied to any regional cost-of-living differences: $6.65 an hour is the same in rural areas and high-cost cities, and the bill contained no small-business tax offset to cushion the payroll increase [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and large for the lowest-paid workers, who would get a raise of $1.50 an hour by the second step. The cost falls on the businesses that employ them, spread across millions of firms, with the strongest argument being possible job or hours losses at the margin. The design is straightforward but blunt — no regional adjustment, no offsetting relief for small employers — which is the honest tradeoff of any flat national wage floor.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate put the bill on its calendar the day after introduction, but the majority leadership never called it up for debate or a vote, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Daschle introduced the bill on January 28, 2003, joined by 37 cosponsors — 36 Democrats and one Independent [S4].
The bill was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 3, which meant it was eligible to be brought to the floor [S3][S5].

No further action was ever taken: no committee hearing, no floor debate, no vote. The action history shows nothing after the January 29 placement on the calendar for the remainder of the 108th Congress [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2005, and the bill expired with it [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who pay the minimum wage came out ahead: they continued paying $5.15 an hour instead of $5.90 and then $6.65, because the bill never reached a vote despite its 37 Senate cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Thomas Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Fair Minimum Wage Act of 2003 on the Senate's first working days and had it placed on the Senate calendar

for.name: 37 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it sufficient Senate support on paper to pass if brought to a vote

against.name: Sen. Bill Frist
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for debate or a vote; bills on the calendar under General Orders reach the floor only when the Majority Leader calls them up

sides.party_line_note: No roll calls occurred, but the bill's sponsorship was entirely Democratic and Independent — 37 of the chamber's minority-party members — while the Republican majority that controlled floor time never scheduled it.

industries.note: These businesses pay the federal minimum wage and would have faced a 30% payroll increase per worker by the second step. Their gain from the bill's failure was lower labor costs, which came at the expense of the lowest-paid workers' paychecks.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands garment and tourism employers
industries.note: The islands had been exempt from the federal minimum wage; the bill would have imposed a $3.55 floor rising to the federal rate. The industry's interest in keeping the exemption ran against the territory's low-wage workers.
Workers earning the $5.15 floor would have gained $1.50 an hour in steps, and Northern Mariana Islands workers would have gained a wage floor for the first time.
